The JET bolometer system (KB5) has one horizontal camera (KB5H) and one vertical camera (KB5V) with 24 bolometer channels each.
The authors collected data from all JET experimental campaigns since the installation of the ITER-like wall in September 2011, resulting in a total of around 18,000 tomographic reconstructions.
The available tomographic reconstructions had a resolution of 115x196 pixels, which the authors padded to 120x200 pixels to facilitate the network design.
Principal component analysis (PCA) showed that 50 components were sufficient to explain 100% of the variance in the 52-channel bolometer input data.
The network was trained using stochastic gradient descent with a learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 10, taking about 17 hours to train on each dataset.

The average structural similarity (SSIM) of the network's reconstructions was 0.98-0.99, the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) was 33-41 dB, and the normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) was 0.02-0.04.

The authors note that the network was able to reproduce the existing tomographic reconstructions with a very low error, indicating that it can match the accuracy of traditional methods based on regularization techniques.
The authors suggest that this deep learning approach could enable real-time tomographic reconstructions to be used as input for the real-time control of fusion experiments.
The authors also note that the approach could be adapted to other tomography diagnostics beyond the JET bolometer system.
The network architecture consisted of two fully-connected layers followed by a series of up-convolutional layers to increase the 1D input to a 2D output image.
The authors conducted preliminary experiments training the network on randomly-generated phantoms, where it was able to reproduce each phantom with an average error per pixel below 2%.
The authors did not observe any significant overfitting during the training process, as the validation loss continued to decrease along with the training loss.
The authors highlight that all tomographic reconstructions can be affected by artifacts due to noise in the projection data or the smoothing constraints applied during the reconstruction process.
The network was able to reproduce not only the inner shape of the plasma, but also the details of the divertor region in the tomographic reconstructions.

The authors note that the up-convolutional network architecture used in this work is the inverse of a typical convolutional neural network (CNN), which usually takes a 2D image as input and produces a 1D output.
